title: Alaska's Fat Bear Week Returns with Record Number of Cubs
summary:
The brown bears of Katmai National Park and Preserve in Alaska are ready for their annual close-up. On Friday, the 2026 Fat Bear Week bracket was released, kicking off a single-elimination tournament to see which bear has packed on the most pounds for hibernation.

This year's bracket features 16 bears, up from 12 in recent years. "There are more cubs at Brooks Camp this year than have been seen in a long time," said Park Superintendent Mark Sturm in a news release. Former park ranger Mike Fitz, now a naturalist at Explore.org, counted 37 cubs at Brooks River.

Fat Bear Week began in 2014 as a way to teach the public about brown bears, sockeye salmon, and their ecosystem. The bears feast on salmon in the Brooks River to prepare for winter, a period of hyperphagia — an intense hunger that helps them store fat. They can bulk up from as little as 600 pounds in spring to over 1,000 pounds in fall.

Some bears have become famous. Last year's winner, Bear 32, nicknamed "Chunk," weighs over 1,200 pounds. He won despite a broken jaw and was even seen playing with younger bears. But he also sparked controversy in 2024 after killing a cub belonging to Grazer, the 2024 champion.

New contenders include Bear 89, called "Backpack," who as a cub had to ride on his mother's back after an injury. Another is Bear 151, known as "Walker," one of the most dominant bears on the river. Bear 806 adopted an older cub while raising her own. Bear 909 lost both her cubs this year but is still preparing for hibernation.

Voting starts Tuesday, September 22, and pauses over the weekend. The champion will be crowned on September 29. Fans can watch the bears on live webcams from Brooks River on Explore.org. Last year, more than 1.7 million votes were cast from over 100 countries.

Ranger Sarah Bruce advised voters: "When you're voting, consider the challenges of a bear's life. Trust your gut and go with whatever you think the fattest bear is."
why_it_matters: Fat Bear Week turns serious biology — salmon runs, hibernation and ecosystem health — into something millions of people follow and argue about, showing how a national park can teach through play. The record number of cubs is also a real signal about how well the river's salmon are doing.

background_read: Katmai National Park and Preserve (a huge national park on the Alaska Peninsula in southwest Alaska) was protected in 1918, partly because of the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, the site of one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the 20th century. Every summer sockeye salmon swim up the Brooks River to lay their eggs, and the bears gather at Brooks Falls to catch them.

Explore.org (a nonprofit that runs live wildlife webcams around the world) streams the Brooks Falls bears, which is how millions of people who will never visit Alaska end up following individual bears by their numbers and nicknames.

Alaska's brown bears are the same species as grizzly bears, but coastal bears grow far bigger because of all the salmon they eat. Fat Bear Week started small in 2014 as a ranger-run online bracket and has grown into a global event that now draws votes from more than 100 countries.

perspectives.description: They see the contest as free publicity that gets millions of people learning about brown bears, salmon and hibernation. The live webcams connect kids and adults to a wild place most of them will never visit in person.

They worry that a popularity contest turns wild animals into mascots, and that the story of a champion killing another bear's cub shows nature is not cute. Extra crowds and cameras at Brooks Falls can also stress the animals.

For them the bracket doubles as a long-running record: a jump to 16 bears and 37 cubs suggests strong salmon runs and a healthy river. The fun event carries real data about how the ecosystem is changing.

As the contest grows global, managers must decide how to keep crowds and cameras from disturbing the bears. They also have to weigh whether the worldwide attention brings money and protection, or just more pressure on a small river.
